newsitem.title: USA: U.S. TV industry submits ratings system to FCC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. TV industry submits ratings system to FCC.

text.p: The television industry and Hollywood on Friday formally submitted to the Federal Communications Commission their controversial system to rate TV shows for sex and violence.

The FCC is expected to issue the ratings for public comment. Under last year's telecommunications law, the FCC must set up and advisory panel to devise a new system if the agency considers the industry plan unacceptable.
The industry has vowed to fight any government-imposed plan in court on First Amendment grounds. President Clinton has said the industry's system should be given a chance before trying to change it.
As outlined last month, the ratings consist of six categories to be shown at the start of programs as a small icon in the upper left-hand corner of the screen.

The submission, in the form of a letter to the FCC, was signed by the presidents of the Motion Picture Association of America, the National Cable Television Association and the National Association of Broadcasers.
Major broadcast and some cable-TV networks already are carrying the ratings.

They are: TV-G, suitable for all ages; TV-PG, parental guidance suggested; TV-14, program may contain material unsuitable for children under 14; and TV-M, mature audiences only. Two categories apply to children's shows: TV-Y for all children and TV-Y7 for kids seven and older.
The ratings have drawn flak from some lawmakers, parent groups, children's advocates, educators and others who argue the new system does not go far enough.
They favor a system that also specifies violence, sex and foul language, using letters such as V, S and L.
